source.title: Exploring Scaling Laws for EHR Foundation Models
source.authors: Sheng Zhang; Qin Liu; N. Usuyama; C. Wong; Tristan Naumann; H. Poon

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling behavior in EHR patient timelines, a non-text modality, and reports compute-optimal allocation and downstream prediction results.
record.gate_note: The study reports an aggregate U-shaped IsoFLOP result and fitted compute-to-optimal-parameter/token power laws. It also reports zero-shot clinical-task results by model size and validation-loss/task-performance relationships. The paper cites language-model scaling results as prior work; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains Llama-architecture models from scratch on MIMIC-IV EHR patient timelines, a non-text sequential modality. It reports its own IsoFLOP profiles and compute-optimal N and D power laws (Hoffmann Approach 2), plus zero-shot clinical-task performance against validation loss and model size. These results bear on V3 and V6 in a new setting and on V5 directly.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that EHR models show LLM-like scaling: parabolic IsoFLOP curves and power-law optimal N (a≈0.58) and D (b≈0.44) vs compute, exponents they say differ from Hoffmann. They also conclude validation loss is a reliable proxy for clinical utility, and that gains saturate beyond 28M parameters, which they attribute to insufficient EHR data.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Hoffmann et al.'s Approach 2 IsoFLOP profiles and validation loss, but applies them to MIMIC-IV patient timelines rather than natural-language pretraining; models use a Llama architecture initialized from scratch, and the paper fits EHR-specific allocation exponents. It does not demonstrate small-run prediction of larger-run loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper attributes the plateau beyond 28M parameters to limited token volume. It notes that EHR modality and the smaller dataset may affect exponent estimates.
record.problems: The authors note that the available EHR token volume is considerably smaller than that in typical LLM studies and may reduce exponent precision and stability. They did not exhaustively sweep training hyperparameters. IsoFLOP fitting retains only the six lowest-loss models per budget, filtering out higher-loss configurations. Downstream performance saturates as model size grows beyond 28M parameters on this dataset.

untested.parts: No loss-vs-N, D or C power law is fitted or reported; only optimal N and D vs C are fitted.
The fitted laws are extrapolated to larger budgets, but no larger run is trained to check the predictions.
Stability beyond about 1.2 orders of magnitude of compute (5e4–8e5 TFLOPs); text language models.
Depth and width are varied only to build size variants; no fixed-parameter shape comparison is reported.
Image, video, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer; also loss-vs-compute power-law form in EHR.
No variation of fitting method, parameter counting or schedule, and no test for curvature. The exponent gap from Hoffmann is only hypothesised, attributed to modality or data scale.

missing.what: Validation loss values of the IsoFLOP minima and per-model losses; no loss-vs-compute fit is reported
Correlation statistic for the log-loss vs task-performance relationship, and per-model validation losses

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V3 'challenges' label is dropped. V3 itself spans Kaplan (N faster) and Hoffmann (equal), so a 0.58/0.44 split is not evidence against V3, and the gap is in a different modality. The V5 limits_scope label was removed because rows r15–r38 measure downstream metrics (V6), not V5's power-law form. Size and compute co-vary for the 1–9M models (each IsoFLOP-optimal at a different budget), while the 28M+ models are early-stopped, so the size comparison is not controlled. The compute range for the exponent fits is only about 16x.

versions.untested_parts: The tested models are EHR models, not language models; the study does not test held-out text-pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens, or compute.
It extrapolates optimal parameter and token counts from IsoFLOP minima, not loss of much larger runs predicted from smaller-run power-law fits.
Tests optimal parameter and token counts versus compute for EHR models; does not establish a universal trend across language-model setups.
Depth, width, and other architecture details are varied to make model variants, but their independent effect on loss at fixed parameter count is not tested.
Tests scaling in EHR timelines only, not image/video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
Tests zero-shot ICU mortality and 30-day readmission performance against validation loss and model size; does not test other downstream task families or language models.
The paper notes its EHR exponents differ from Hoffmann et al. and offers possible modality/data explanations, but does not vary fitting choices or test whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: EHR foundation models trained on MIMIC-IV patient timelines
rows.size_stated: Model configurations from 1M to 982M parameters are discussed; six lowest-loss models retained per IsoFLOP profile.
rows.operation_detail: Trained models at varied parameter counts under fixed FLOP budgets and compared validation loss across model sizes.
rows.measure: Validation loss versus parameter count at fixed compute (IsoFLOP profile)
rows.value: For each tested FLOP budget, the loss had a well-defined U-shaped profile with a loss-optimal model size.
rows.note: Aggregate result across the tested compute budgets; the paper says it plotted the six lowest-validation-loss models for each budget.
rows.check: Only the six lowest-loss models per budget were plotted and fitted, so the U-shape is shown on a filtered subset. There are five budgets spanning 5e4–8e5 TFLOPs, a 16x range (about 1.2 orders of magnitude). No loss values are given.

source_check.correct: Observed for V3: parabolic IsoFLOP profiles fitted to the six lowest-loss models per budget. Remove the V5 link: these profiles do not establish a power-law relationship between held-out loss and resources.
source_check.problem: The observed state fits V3; the measure cannot establish V5's loss power-law extension.

rows.operation_detail: Related downstream task performance to validation loss across models.
rows.value: ROC AUC improves from 0.68 to 0.75 as validation loss drops from 1.0 to 0.85.
rows.note: The text presents this as an example of a strong linear correlation between log validation loss and task performance.
rows.check: The text attributes ROC 0.68→0.75 to ICU mortality. Those values match the 30-day readmission range in Fig. 4 (0.679–0.747), while the ICU ROCs in Fig. 3 span 0.635–0.902. The task label is likely mislabelled in the paper. No correlation coefficient is given.
